exploration.title: Bridge Builder
exploration.subject: Engineering
exploration.summary: Add braces, move a load and compare how a bridge carries weight to its supports.
exploration.question: Why can the same load be harder to support in the middle of a bridge?
exploration.explanation: A bridge transfers a load to its supports. The load can bend the span; diagonal braces form triangles that help a frame resist changing shape. Materials and reinforcement affect what a structure can carry and how much it costs. This model calculates a simple beam’s bending and uses invented brace strengths and costs for comparison. Its capacity-use display is not a real bridge safety rating, and it does not calculate every force in a truss.

experiments.title: Move the load
experiments.instruction: Keep material, load size and braces fixed. Predict whether the middle or near an end will bend the span more, then move the load across.
experiments.observe: Compare the capacity-use readings and force on each support. Explain why moving weight changes how the load is carried.

experiments.title: Place a brace where it helps
experiments.instruction: Keep the load in the middle. Predict which brace will reduce the highest capacity-use reading, then add braces one at a time.
experiments.observe: Compare each section’s capacity use and the material cost. Explain which brace helped at this load position, then test whether it still helps when the load moves.

exploration.misconception: A triangular shape is not a guarantee of safety. Connections, materials, loads and many other conditions matter in a real bridge.
